stories.title: €8bn in bailout loans to be repaid early under Govt plans
stories.summary: The Government is planning to repay €8 billion in loans received during the financial crisis ahead of schedule. The proposed repayments relate to loans provided under the European Financial Stabilisation Mechanism (EFSM) as part of the country's EU-IMF bailout programme. Tánaiste and Minister for Finance Simon Harris brought a memo to the Cabinet this week, which will allow the State to make early repayments on the State's loans, in a move that could save the taxpayer an estimated €90m. Ireland originally borrowed €22.5 billion under the EFSM, with €15.3 billion currently outstanding. The exact details of the loan agreement will be announced in the coming days following consultation at both a domestic and EU level. The move will be seen as significant as it will reduce Ireland's national debt at a time when interest rates are rising.

stories.title: Renewed appeal over murder of David Nunan 21 years ago
stories.summary: Gardaí have renewed their appeal for information into the murder of 25-year-old David Nunan, whose body was found in Co Clare more than 21 years ago. Mr Nunan's body was discovered by a farmer tending to cattle near a laneway in the Fairyhill area of Parteen on 28 October 2005. A post-mortem examination confirmed he had died from gunshot wounds, and a murder investigation was launched at Mayorstone Garda Station. On the night of his death, Mr Nunan had been playing video games with a friend at his home in O'Malley Park, Limerick. At around 2am, he received a phone call and, after finishing the call, told his friend he was going for a spin in a car. Gardaí believe a wine-coloured Toyota Carina may have collected him from his home and travelled from Southill to Moyross, before heading towards Parteen, where the murder took place.

stories.title: Ireland has 'no intention of joining NATO' - Taoiseach
stories.summary: Taoiseach Micheál Martin has insisted Ireland has "no intention of joining NATO", despite former president Michael D Higgins warning that Ireland risks "sliding" into losing its neutrality if the Triple Lock is removed. In an interview with the Irish Examiner on Saturday, after last week's initial Dail vote to remove the Triple Lock, Mr Higgins said the Government was not being honest about what may happen and that Ireland could slide into international military alliances. However, responding to that view at the launch of the Government's rural Ireland plan 2026-2031, the Taoiseach said the situation has been misrepresented. Asked about former president Higgins' comments, the Taoiseach asked "what military alliance?", before insisting when NATO was referenced that Ireland "has no intention of joining NATO". Mr Martin said he is asked every few years about the issue, and that in his view Ireland is "militarily neutral", arguing it was incorrect to suggest the EU is "war mongering" - a label he said some Opposition parties have made both now and in previous decades. The Taoiseach said that "for the first time in 10 years" and arguably in a generation "the UN Security Council is dysfunctional".

stories.title: ECB to keep rates steady amid focus on French bonds
stories.summary:
The European Central Bank is set to keep interest rates on hold today in a well-telegraphed decision that is likely to be overshadowed by questions about bond-market turmoil ⁠in France and ECB President Christine Lagarde's own future. The euro zone's central bank has already raised rates twice since June and is expected to resume tightening in the coming months as policymakers seek to prevent an oil-price shock linked to the Iran war from feeding into other prices and wages. But it must also contend with a surge in government bond yields - especially in debt-laden France - that has pushed up borrowing costs for households and businesses and which Lagarde has said will curb growth and inflation. Caught between persistent inflation fuelled by a renewed surge in energy costs and deteriorating financing conditions, the ECB is widely expected to keep its deposit rate at 2.5% while signalling that another increase, potentially as soon as December, remains likely. "There is likely a low bar to another hike in December, given the likelihood of another upward revision of the ECB's inflation forecast due to higher energy prices," Oliver Rakau at Oxford Economics said
.
Such an outlook is consistent with signals from the US Federal Reserve, which left rates unchanged last night but kept the door ‌open to more tightening, solidifying market bets for an early December ⁠move. Money markets are currently pricing another three rate increases from the ECB by the end of next year, which would take the deposit rate to 3.25%, a level that is widely seen as restricting economic growth.

stories.title: Girl, 8, attacked by wolf in German wildlife park
stories.summary: A young girl has been attacked by a wolf and badly injured in a German wildlife park, police said, adding that the eight-year-old was taken to hospital by rescue helicopter. "The girl was attacked and seriously injured by at least one wolf within an animal enclosure while she was there with two other children and a staff member," police said. They added in a statement that "the precise circumstances of the incident are the subject of an ongoing police investigation". The attack took place in the town of Baruth/Mark south of the capital Berlin, police said, adding that the staff member and other children were not injured. The park keeps brown bears, lynx and grey and arctic wolves, according to its website, which said that the facility was temporarily closed without providing further details.

stories.summary: Former Dublin star Ciarán Kilkenny has given his endorsement for the experimental four-point goal rule that has been in place in the early weeks of the college Gaelic football season. A series of new rules - separate to the now not-so-new rules introduced in 2025 - have been used in the early weeks of the college season with the four-point goal among them. Gaelic football's Expert Advisory Group (EAG), chaired by former Roscommon and Mayo boss Kevin McStay, introduced 11 updated rules to be monitored during the Ryan Cup with around 15 third-level games to be assessed. It is hoped the extra reward for raising a green flag will negate any anticipated over-reliance on shooting from distance since the introduction of the two-point arc. Small sample size though it may be, Kilkenny - now in charge of Technological University Dublin (TUD) - sees merit in the four-pointer and feels the excitement of the ball hitting the back of the net is something that every fan wants to see. "It takes a bit of time. It took us probably a game or two to get used to it actually being four and counting it up when you're doing the scoreboard."

stories.title: Fleetwood dump PL champions Arsenal out of Carabao Cup
stories.summary: League Two Fleetwood shocked Premier League champions Arsenal in a penalty shoot-out to advance to the Carabao Cup quarter-finals after a 1-1 draw. Bruno Guimaraes saw his spot-kick saved by Jay Lynch before Fleetwood's teenage defender Conor Haughey lashed home an emphatic penalty to spark a pitch invasion at Highbury Stadium as Fleetwood triumphed 5-3 in one of the greatest upsets in the competition’s history. There's a strong Irish connection to Fleetwood with manager Matt Lawlor formerly taking charge of Waterford FC in 2025. Limerick's Ronan Coughlan, who played for a multitude of League of Ireland clubs, scored in the shoot-out and Haughey plays for the Northern Ireland Under-21s. "Amazing for the club, the town. Honestly it means everything to everyone," Lynch told Sky. "We took heart from Grimsby beating Man Utd last year. We kind of compared it. The whole team throughout the game was magnificent. To beat the English champions - credit to these lads." Fleetwood, 18th in League Two, dared to dream after Fulham loanee Aaron Loupalo-Bi put them in front after 21 minutes against a much-changed Arsenal side struggling to find any fluidity on the Fylde coast.

stories.title: No Kolbe, Etzebeth or Pollard as Erasmus names Boks squad
stories.summary: South Africa head coach Rassie Erasmus will be without the services of World Cup winning trio, Cheslin Kolbe, Eben Etzebeth and Handre Pollard for the Nations Championship, while Argentina have also been hit by injuries ahead of their opener against Ireland. The Springboks - who come to Dublin on 21 November - will assemble next week ahead of a three-game window against Italy, France and Ireland, before the Nations Championship finals weekend in Twickenham at the end of November. If the reigning World Cup, Rugby Championship and Greatest Rivalry winners are to claim the inaugural Nations Championship crown, they will do so without marquee stars Kolbe, Etzebeth and Pollard. Their 33-year-old outside back Kolbe has not featured since the third test against New Zealand in September, while lock Etzebeth played for the Sharks against Leinster and the Stormers in the URC, but is unavailable. Out-half Pollard started in the Bulls' 34-26 win over Ulster at the weekend but is nursing an injury, while centre Andre Esterhuizen, who also misses out, was helped off the field in the Sharks' win in Edinburgh last Friday. Erasmus has included six new call-ups in his 37-man group: Yaqeen Ahmed, Sebastian de Klerk, Luan Giliomee, Markus Muller, Riley Norton, and Emmanuel Tshituka all get the nod.

stories.title: Five albums to put you in the spooky mood this Halloween
stories.summary: A change of season always brings a shift in mood. As much as I mourn the death of summer, I'm overcome by giddy excitement for Halloween, writes Darragh MacManus. In celebration of All Hallows' Eve, I have compiled my five of my favourite albums to put you in the spooky mood... This Galwegian three-piece have gone from strength to strength, including selling out shows as far afield as Tokyo. MADRA has a ghostly atmosphere that is perfect for the falling of leaves. It is brilliantly balanced between sinister riffs on "Let Go" and ethereal vocals on "White Ribbons", while "Nightmares" is an outstanding song about how toxic relationships can twist your perception of reality. This is a fantastic indie-rock album with paranormal energy that feels ideal for this time of year. The title and album cover say it all. Nigerian born, Tallaght raised rapper Travy opens his debut LP with apocalyptic choirs and heavy-hitting 808s. His flow is aggressive and ambitious, matching the menacing beats superbly. "EUROSTAR" has an ominous feel, accentuated with eerie bells and strong features from French rapper Yvnnis and Dundalk native Reggie. "Conversations" is another standout track, with its swirling pianos and catchy outro. This is horror-movie Irish rap at its best. You have probably heard "Insomniac" via your Spotify For You Page, but I promise you this album has so much more to offer. Otto Benson, aka Memo Boy, captured a vibe in his Brooklyn bedroom as a teenager - a twisting maze of Aphex Twin-inspired IDM and lo-fi synth pop - that I haven't heard replicated before or since. The melodies are moody, the synths are brooding and the overall atmosphere is seriously uneasy. I would encourage you to listen to "Brian is the Most Beautiful", "I’m Having a Rave in My Room All By Myself" and my personal favourite "Batman Loathes Himself and Vomits". Like the paper-mache mask on its cover, this album falls into the uncanny valley. Some music resists being forced into the confines of a genre. This album embodies emotions of hopelessness and isolation. Corbin’s voice is raw and fragile. There is a palpable sense of pain poured into these songs. This is heard best on "All Out", which captures a profound sense of regret. It is possibly the darkest album on this list, but exceptional all the same.

Dublin Independent Fashion Week will serve iconic fashion moments at The Big Romance on Friday, 30 October. Taking place at The Circular, there will be spooky music followed by a fancy dress competition and a night of dancing. Taking place on Saturday, 31 October, from 7pm - 11:30pm. Tickets €10. stories.title: Deadly train crash in Spain raises safety concerns
stories.summary: Spain's second high-speed rail disaster this year, a crash in which one train struck another from behind, killing 68 people, has raised fresh concerns about the safety of the country's rail network. Yesterday, 68 people died in the train crash and Spain's health minister Monica Garcia said that 80 people were injured, 15 of them very seriously. Spain's network of high-speed rail has been considered one of the nation's crowning achievements. It ranks second to China in track mileage in the world, and until this year, it had not endured a deadly crash since coming into service more than three decades ago. But the collision, which turned a sleepy stretch of railway lined by olive groves into a scene of carnage, came just four weeks before the country votes in a national election. Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez visited the crash site in the central province of Toledo after regional authorities confirmed that 68 people had died and dozens more were being treated at hospitals. Josimar Medina, a 31-year-old Peruvian who was holidaying in Spain with his girlfriend, said he was sleeping on the Renfe train when "I woke up and I was in the air".

stories.title: Job hunt 'impossible' for Ukrainians with disabilities
stories.summary: Organisations supporting Ukrainian refugees in Ireland have warned of a potential rise in homelessness due to the withdrawal by the Government of State accommodation. Minister for Justice Jim O'Callaghan has estimated that there will be a projected reduction of €430 million in accommodation spending for Ukrainians in 2027, equivalent to 71% and the process of ending over 140 accommodation contracts is currently under way. The Government transition away from temporary protection has raised concern for Ukrainian refugees who have disabilities in particular. Pavlo Romaniuk and Yuliia Nahaiets arrived in Ireland three years ago under the EU's temporary protection programme. stories.title: Enforcement of flavoured vapes ban could take a year
stories.summary: New legislation banning the sale of flavoured vapes and restrictions on eye-catching packaging have officially been signed into law, though full enforcement could take up to a year. President Catherine Connolly today signed the Public Health (Tobacco Products and Nicotine Inhaling Products) (Amendment) Bill 2026 into law after it passed all stages of the Oireachtas. Under the legislation, the sale of nicotine inhaling products with flavours such as menthol or fruity varieties will be banned. Colourful or eye-catching imagery on their packaging is also prohibited under the legislation. The laws also empower the Minister for Health to regulate flavour names. It also introduces restrictions on signage, display and advertising of nicotine inhaling products in shops and online.

stories.title: Fed leaves rates unchanged as it awaits more information
stories.summary: The US Federal Reserve held interest rates steady last night, as expected, opting to delay any changes to borrowing costs until after next week's US midterm elections while it awaits further data on inflation, which the central bank said "remains elevated." The 10-2 decisionto maintain the Fed's benchmark interest rate within the 3.75%-4% range came with an upgraded assessment of an economy that the central bank now says is growing at a "strong pace." Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh also expressed confidence that inflation can be lowered to the 2% target without having to "throw sand in the gears" and slow growth or raise unemployment. Kevin Warsh, speaking at a press conference after the end of a two-day policy meeting, said he expects a report on third-quarter gross domestic product today to show strong investment and consumer spending and an acceleration of growth from the first half of the year. Warsh, however, said he still does not think the economy is "too hot" or generating demand-side inflation that needs to be curbed. "The economy is pointing in the right direction. Is the economy running too hot? Is the economy running too strong? That isn't the judgment of most of my colleagues," said Warsh, arguing, as he has before, that changes in productivity, even predating the artificial intelligence boom, may allow the US to grow faster without as much inflation.

stories.summary: Russell Brand told jurors at his rape trial he has dedicated much of his life to "beyond reckless philandering and idiocy", and admitted he had been wrong to use his fame to get sex. The 51-year-old gave evidence for more than four hours at London's Southwark Crown Court, insisting that "consent is more important than sex itself" and issuing a string of denials to the charges he faces. He is accused of raping women in a hotel room, at his home, and in a bar toilet, and other women have accused Mr Brand of sexually assaulting them in a recording studio and a radio station corridor. Mr Brand told jurors he now believes it was "wrong" that he used his fame in the 2000s to "facilitate sexual access". "As I became more successful and famous I was very comfortable allowing that to facilitate sexual access which I agree with you was wrong," he said. As his evidence concluded, he said: "I do recognise I have been a very determined and focused man.

stories.title: Laid-back farmer McNabney raring to go after Irish recall
stories.summary: For a young man of just 23, it feels like James McNabney's road to an Ireland shirt is already one of the most winding routes of anyone in the squad. His family is not steeped in the game, although his uncle Sam captained the Cambridge House Grammar School's first team. It was there that nephew James first picked up a rugby ball, aged 11, perhaps driven by his sheer size and farmer strength. He was lining out for the Ireland Under-20s just shy of his 19th birthday, and after back-to-back Grand Slam successes and a trip to the 2023 Under-20 World Championship final, under the tutelage of Richie Murphy, the Ulster man was tipped for great things. McNabney played 17 times for Ulster in the 2024/25 campaign, earning a call-up to Ireland's summer tests against Georgia and Portugal. He looked destined for a debut, but disaster struck in the most innocuous fashion. "I was just in training, and I sidestepped, planted hard with a leg, and I just heard the pop and that was it," McNabney explained. He had surgery on 8 June 2025, and did not play another minute of rugby until 4 September 2026, a span of 454 days.

stories.title: Forde reflects on 'pride' of earning historic All-Star
stories.summary: The 2026 All Star awards will be handed out at the RDS next Friday night, with All-Ireland football champions Mayo and their hurling counterparts Limerick likely to dominate the two selections. Most players covet the Celtic Cross, but for some who haven't had the chance to play in an All-Ireland final, an All-Star award can be the highlight of a career. Wexford is one of a handful of counties that has only ever won one football All-Star; it arrived in 2004, when Matty Forde was at the peak of his powers. The Kilanerin-Ballyfad forward finished as the championship’s top scorer that season, despite only having five outings throughout the course of the campaign. stories.title: UCD dispatch Longford to set up Bray showdown
stories.summary: UCD's safe passage to Sunday’s SSE Airtricity Men's First Division play-off final was never in doubt as they eased past Longford Town at the UCD Bowl. Already 2-0 up after the first leg, College barely broke sweat as goals in each half from Mikey McCullagh and Hugh Smith completed a straightforward victory that will keep their season alive for another game at least. The Students will face Bray Wanderers in Sunday’s division final at Tolka Park (3.00pm) with the winner progressing to face the ninth-placed team in the Premier Division - currently Drogheda United - for the right to play in the top flight next season. The onus was on Longford to come out fighting, but they never looked capable of inflicting the sort of damage needed to get themselves back into this tie. Darragh Murtagh was put through early on but his shot from a decent position in the box clipped defender Harry Curtis and went out for a corner. Murtagh then fizzed another effort over the crossbar from further out but Longford's attacking play lacked conviction when it mattered - and UCD showed their First Division rivals how to pack a punch with the lead goal after 19 minutes.

stories.title: McMillan: Coombes not dwelling on Furlong incident
stories.summary: Munster head coach Clayton McMillan has said that Gavin Coombes has returned to business as normal, following the incident in Saturday's defeat to Leinster that led to Tadhg Furlong being cited. The Leinster prop was accused of interfering with the groin area of Coombes during a first half ruck, although no on-field action was taken due to a lack of replays. For Coombes, however, he returned to the HPC in Limerick as normal according to his head coach. "Nothing has changed for Gavin (Coombes), he turned up on Monday," McMillan said on Tuesday. "What happened on the weekend is now in the hands of the judicial committee. "Like the rest of the group, he's just turned up and focused on preparing for the Sharks this weekend, allowing whatever happens in the background to take care of itself."

stories.title: Breast cancer at 27: "You really have to advocate for yourself"
stories.summary: To mark Breast Cancer Awareness Month, Charlotte Ryan speaks to Alanna Kells about being diagnosed with breast cancer at 27 and how advocating for herself played a vital role in being treated. "I'm a very health-conscious person", Kells, a 28-year-old woman living in Cavan, tells me early into our chat. "I booked my smear test on my 25th birthday. I do my hygienist, my dentist, my opticians every six months." Part of that wellbeing routine, she says, was checking her breasts for signs of breast cancer even if she didn't expect to find them. "The way I always describe it, it's like you check your smoke detector, but you never think there's actually going to be a fire. I was doing breast checks but never thinking it would ever actually be a problem. It's just something you're meant to do, so I was doing it." However, one night when lying on her side, she noticed a new pearl-sized lump in her breast. Kells had, from a medical point of view, done everything 'right' when it comes to lifestyle: she's a regular gym-goer, a vegetarian and a non-smoker. She also had no genetic predisposition to breast cancer, as a lengthy genetic panel showed. No one in her family, barring an aunt in her late 50s, had ever had breast cancer.

stories.title: 26% of adults have experienced sexual violence - report
stories.summary: Just over a quarter (26%) of the population have experienced sexual violence as an adult, according to a report. Women, younger adults, bisexual individuals and gay men face significantly higher risks, while most perpetrators are known to victims, the report found. The research published by the Economic and Social Research Institute (ESRI) and Cuan, as part of their Joint Research Programme on Adult Sexual Violence in Ireland, provides new evidence on the factors associated with experiences of sexual violence among adults in Ireland. Drawing on data from the 2022 Central Statistics Office Sexual Violence Survey, the report examines patterns of adult sexual violence, including both intimate partner and non-intimate partner sexual violence. The research provides detailed analyses to date of the population groups most at risk of sexual violence and the circumstances in which sexual violence occurs. It found that sexual violence affects a substantial proportion of adults in Ireland, however, the risks of victimisation are not evenly distributed across the population.

stories.title: No cost-of-living payment for NI without budget - Bryant
stories.summary: Northern Ireland is set to miss out on a cost-of-living payment included in an additional £270 million for the region unless Stormont ministers can agree a budget, the UK's Northern Secretary Chris Bryant has indicated. Stormont Executive parties have all said they have been unable to agree a budget, more than halfway through this current financial year, due to a lack of funding. Mr Bryant said that with Northern Ireland departments limited to 95% of last year's spend, and missing out on additional money on offer, agreeing a budget "is a no-brainer". He said he would be speaking with the Stormont Executive parties by phone today, pressing them to agree a budget, and will meet in person if necessary. He suggested £270m in Barnett consequentials for Stormont is more than he had expected would come, clarifying it will be an extra £131m to spend in this financial year. That includes funding to extend the £100 cost-of-living payment to lower income households in Northern Ireland.

stories.title: Where to next after Triple Lock passes first Dáil vote?
stories.summary: The 'Triple Lock' has become one of the most contentious topics in this Government's Programme for Government, in Dáil Éireann, within the Fianna Fáil party and on the streets. But it all began when legislation was passed in 1960 to allow Irish troops to be sent abroad, after joining the United Nations five years previously. These missions would only be backed by the United Nations and for decades that meant Irish participation in peacekeeping has depended on UN backing. This rule was restated as the 'Triple Lock' at the start of the century after concerns that the Nice and Lisbon Treaties would undermine neutrality, with Government parties back then stressing its importance. Under the rule, no more than 12 troops can be deployed on an active mission overseas without a decision by the Government, the approval of the Dáil and the authorisation of the United Nations. However, because the Government usually has a majority in the Dáil, the first two conditions are largely one and the same, and UN approval became key.

stories.title: Microsoft's cloud growth, cash flow offer AI respite
stories.summary: Microsoft last night delivered a big cash flow beat and forecast strong cloud growth, offering fresh evidence that its hefty AI bets were paying off even as concerns mount over Big Tech's spending spree. The results underscore a widening financial divide among the industry's biggest AI spenders, as soaring infrastructure costs force some rivals to turn more heavily to capital markets. Microsoft's shares rose more than 3% in after-hours trading. The company posted market-beating 48% growth in its Azure cloud business in its fiscal first quarter ended September, and generated $18.6 billion in free cash flow - some $10 billion more than analysts expected. That financial firepower set the maker of the Windows operating system apart from rivals such as Alphabet and Meta, whose heavy AI investments have squeezed free cash flow and increased their reliance on borrowing. Alphabet reported negative free cash flow of $9.07 billion in the third quarter as capital spending jumped and growth in its core ad business slowed, overshadowing a doubling of its cloud sales and sending its shares down 8% in extended trading. Meta last week posted its first cash burn in more than a decade, and said it planned to issue new stock to fund its growing capital costs.

stories.title: Stranded cruise passengers seek investor to continue trip
stories.summary: Passengers of a cruise ship stuck in Cambodia after it ran out of fuel are waiting to see if an investor will finance the rest of the trip, one of the stranded passengers has said. Around 200 passengers who paid to live on the Odyssey cruise ship, which set off from Belfast two years ago, have been abruptly left in a Cambodian port after the company ran out of money. US-based operator Villa Vie Residences announced yesterday it had "suspended operations in Cambodia" as it worked to address "extraordinary increases" in fuel costs following the Iran war. Holly Hennessey said that she has spent just under half a million dollars since first boarding the Odyssey in 2024. She said that the cruise "ran out of money" and "all the passengers were asked to disembark". "So there are possibilities. The fat lady is singing, but she hasn't finished the song just yet."

stories.summary: The Milwaukee Brewers have won their first World Series with a 4-1 victory over the Tampa Bay Rays in game five. A single from Cooper Pratt sent Brice Turang home to put Milwaukee ahead at the top of the second inning, before the Brewers added another score in the fifth off a David Hamilton hit. They doubled their lead in their next at-bat through a double from William Contreras and Pratt's sacrifice-fly. The Rays were finally able to get on the scoreboard in the ninth, but Milwaukee's pitcher Jacob Misiorowski slammed the door shut with a stellar effort on the mound. He gave up just one run on four hits with three strikeouts and a walk over his five innings. Chandler Simpson was the sole Ray to make an impact with the bat, sending Liam Hicks home off a double.
